content.p: Arthur Stanley Smith, known to Sydney as Neddy, was one of the best-known criminals in Australia and one of the last who made no secret of what he was. In the 1970s and 1980s he could be found drinking in Sydney pubs, and he gave television interviews. He traded in heroin, robbed for a living and, by his own account, bought protection from senior police. He died in Long Bay prison hospital on 8 September 2021, aged 76, still serving two life sentences for murder.

He was charged with eight murders and convicted of two: the killing of a tow-truck driver in a street quarrel, and the shooting of a brothel owner. He was acquitted of a third, the killing of the whistleblower Sallie-Anne Huckstepp. After his own arrest he gave evidence about corrupt detectives to two inquiries into the New South Wales police, and his partnership with the detective Roger Rogerson became the subject of a television drama.

Smith was born in Sydney on 27 November 1944, the son of an Australian mother and a US serviceman he never met. The smh.com.au obituary says he had three half-brothers, each with a different father. The ABC reported that he grew up in boys' homes known for their brutality and was first arrested at 11. The smh.com.au article said he was convicted of stealing at that age and sent to a boys' home at Mittagong, left school at 13, and was arrested at 14 for attempted break and enter. By 16, the smh.com.au article said, he was living with a prostitute and pimping for her, and by 18 he had seven convictions.

The record that followed was long. He was jailed for armed robbery and, at 22, for taking part in a gang rape, for which he received 12 years. He served seven and was released in 1975. Reports of his prison terms put them at 1963 to 1965, 1968 to 1975 and 1978 to 1980, then from 1989 until his death. Accounts disagree on his height. The reports give it as 6ft 2in, 6ft 5in, 6ft 6in and 1.98 metres. They agree that he was a large and frightening man, and a prisoners' advocate who met him in Maitland jail in 1973 said he had become dangerous because of the way he had been treated.

In the 1970s Smith worked as a standover man, an enforcer, for Murray Riley, a former Olympic medallist and police officer who had turned to drug trafficking. The crime reporter Stephen Gibbs told Central News that the heroin that flooded into Australia in the 1980s changed the business: men who had done armed robberies moved into drug importation, which was lucrative and safer. Smith moved with them. The ABC reported that in 1978 he and his wife Debra were arrested for importing heroin from Thailand, and that Smith claimed he paid off police to have the charges diluted. Three other Australians arrested in Bangkok received heavy prison terms in a Thai jail.

In the 1980s he led a gang that, according to the Guardian, was alleged to have been responsible for crime worth $25 million. John Laycock, a retired assistant police commissioner who headed Task Force Snowy, a police inquiry into 14 gangland murders linked to Smith, told the ABC that in his heyday Smith was number one and was turning over millions in drug money, exporting, selling and distributing it with his own network of runners and dealers.

His methods were brutal. A Sydney criminal-law firm's profile described a dispute with a rival crew in the mid-1980s in which Smith knocked out the son of a Chippendale publican and then beat five bouncers with a baseball bat at gunpoint. The smh.com.au article listed a man whose ear he bit off, a payroll robbery, and a club security officer he and his associate Graham "Abo" Henry beat so badly that the man partly lost the sight of an eye.

The central claim in Smith's story concerns the police. In the autobiography he wrote with the journalist Tom Noble, Neddy, he said he had what criminals called the "Green Light", meaning "I could do anything I pleased". He wrote: "Thank Christ for corruption! I couldn't have survived without it." The smh.com.au article noted that Rogerson, then a detective sergeant, was one of his most notorious associations, and the ABC reported that Rogerson recruited him as an informant in 1976.

The turning point, in Smith's telling, came on 27 June 1981. Smith escorted a heroin dealer, Warren Lanfranchi, to a meeting with Rogerson in a Chippendale laneway. Lanfranchi died there. A coroner's jury concluded that Rogerson shot him while attempting to arrest him, and the smh.com.au article recorded that there was much suspicion about the incident, directed at other police as well as Rogerson. In New Matilda's 2005 interview, Smith said Lanfranchi was unarmed and that he himself had held the gun. Smith said that because he told investigators nothing that endangered the police involved, he received his green light afterward. He also claimed that police once diverted traffic so he could carry out a robbery.

The Wood Royal Commission, whose report appeared in 1997, found that "a trade-off was established with Mr Arthur Stanley (Neddy) Smith for him to receive a 'green light' to perform armed robberies", according to Central News. The commission found the arrangement extended further, to assault, robbery and heroin trafficking, Central News said. Lanfranchi's girlfriend, Sallie-Anne Huckstepp, spoke publicly about the relationship between Rogerson and Smith.

Huckstepp's body was found in a pond in Centennial Park in 1986; New Matilda gives the date of the killing as 6 February. The case has not been officially solved. Smith was charged with her murder and acquitted, and New Matilda says the Crown case relied partly on conversations secretly taped between Smith and a cellmate. The Sydney law firm's profile said that on those tapes Smith boasted of involvement in seven more murders, though he later said he had made it up because he knew he was being recorded. In a prison interview with the author of a book on Huckstepp, Smith said he had not been there and had been home with his wife. He told the author that he knew his cellmate was an informer and boasted on the tape only to publicise his book, Catch and Kill Your Own. He blamed another man, whom he refused to name. The author's view is that confessions to a crime he did not commit would be an expensive form of publicity, since they helped to produce his second murder conviction. No court has found who killed Huckstepp.

By the mid-1980s the protection was fraying. According to Gangsters Inc, Rogerson went on national television in April 1986 and outed Smith as an informant, and a hit and run the following night left Smith badly hurt. The ABC and Gangsters Inc both list a broken leg, eight fractured ribs, two spinal fractures and a broken collar bone. Smith survived another attempt on his life outside the Iron Duke Hotel in Alexandria, according to the smh.com.au article.

In October 1987 he killed Ronnie Flavell, a 34-year-old tow-truck driver, at a busy intersection on Coogee Bay Road. The Sydney Crime Museum gives the date as 30 October 1987 and says it followed a long drinking session with Rogerson across several pubs. Reports differ on what set it off. The ABC says Flavell had flashed his headlights at Smith, who was double parked; Gangsters Inc says there was a collision with the tow truck. The commentator Gibbs said it was unclear what happened that night, but that drink and a violent temper were behind it. The ABC and Gangsters Inc say Smith stabbed Flavell as onlookers watched. The Guardian wrote instead that he ran Flavell down, and one law-firm profile says he bashed him and dates it 1988. The Pilbara News calls the crime a murder in company. The smh.com.au obituary dates the killing to October 1987 and says it earned him life imprisonment.

Smith was picked up outside Botany Council on 22 December 1988, according to the Sydney Crime Museum, planning to hit its Christmas payroll (put at $160,000 by Central News), and he was refused bail on the Flavell charge. He was in prison from 1989. Accounts date his life sentence to 1989 or 1990.

A string of drug-related murders was thought by police to be linked to Smith, and they bugged his cell in Long Bay, recording his conversations with a fellow inmate known in court as Mr Brown. Smith was charged with seven further murders. Four other cases, over the deaths of Danny Chubb, Barry McCann, Barry Croft and Bruce Sandery, did not get past committal, and he was indicted over the death of a drug dealer, Lewton Shu, but was not to face trial for it, the smh.com.au piece of 2003 reported. He went to trial for two: Huckstepp and Harvey Jones.

Jones was last seen leaving the Star Hotel in Alexandria with Smith in 1983; his body was found buried near Botany years later. The Guardian dates the discovery to 1995. The law-firm profile says Mr Brown testified that Smith told him he had shot Jones in the hotel cellar and taken the body to Botany Bay. Smith was found guilty in 1998, the Guardian and the profile both report, and received his second life sentence. Under truth-in-sentencing rules he expected never to be released.

After his arrest Smith decided to speak. The profile dates his appearance as a star witness at the Independent Commission Against Corruption to 1992, where he and Henry described how former Armed Holdup Squad detectives had passed on information that helped them commit robberies in the 1980s. ABC News reported that he said he had paid tens of thousands of dollars in bribes to some of the force's most senior detectives, and was offered indemnity for a number of crimes in New South Wales. The commissioner, Ian Temby QC, found the Smith-Rogerson relationship "notorious" and wrote that Rogerson's dealings with Smith "brought discredit on the Police Service, and must be described as scandalous". Smith refused to name Rogerson at the hearing, the profile says.

The smh.com.au article noted that Smith's credibility with the commission was low and that Temby made positive findings only on statements that could be independently corroborated. It added that the Wood commission put paid to doubts about widespread corruption. Gibbs saw an element of getting square: when corrupt police could no longer save him, he decided to bring some of them down with him. When Rogerson later faced his former associate's evidence, Gangsters Inc said, he called Smith a "dog". Rogerson was later jailed for life for the 2014 murder of Jamie Gao, the Guardian said.
content.h2: Blue Murder, family, and the final years
content.p: Smith and Rogerson were portrayed in the 1995 ABC miniseries Blue Murder, with Tony Martin playing Smith. The series was held back in New South Wales for six years until the court cases involving Smith were finished, the Canberra Times reported. His former wife Debra, whom he married in Long Bay when she was 22 and he 12 years older, objected to two scenes, including one showing her slapping him, and said he would not have tolerated Henry waving a gun in front of children. They had three children and by 2003 were divorced; he had by then been moved to Lithgow prison. She said she had been horrified to learn of the drug money.

He wrote two books about the underworld, Neddy and Catch and Kill Your Own, the second of which he later said he had used for publicity. In 2008 his Parkinson's medication stopped working effectively. A 2010 request to serve out his sentence under house arrest was refused; he said then, through his lawyers, "I'm not guilty, my health is not good, and I've done my time". Laycock said the only way Smith should leave prison was horizontal. In 2017, aged 72, Smith was admitted to the cardiac ward at the Prince of Wales Hospital in Randwick, where two guards were investigated after he was reportedly found by nurses in a hallway, apparently trying to pull out his drip. The Guardian reported the minister said the prospect of his escape sent a chill down his spine.

Smith died on 8 September 2021 at Long Bay Hospital at about 5.20 p.m. The ABC reported that he had dementia and that it was understood he died of natural causes. Corrective Services NSW noted that all deaths in custody are subject to a coronial inquest. The former detective and author Duncan McNab said Smith was an "absolutely appalling human being": a violent offender, a rapist and a murderer who had at one time been the country's biggest heroin dealer.
